study.title: Psalm 4 Peace in the midst of anguish and trust in the Lord
study.overview: This psalm of David presents a short and intense prayer that goes from distress to serenity. The psalmist begins by asking that God hear him in his anguish, he faces the opposition of the "childmen of men," calls the faithful to integrity and trust, denounces the empty search for happiness in passing things and ends with a calm certainty: he can lie down and sleep in peace because the Lord himself sustains him in safety. The movement of the Psalm shows that biblical peace is not born from the absence of conflict, but from God's favorable presence.

outline.title: Clamor by response and separation to God
outline.explanation: David asks for mercy and attentive ear, while confronting those who treat his honor with contempt and love the lie. In contrast, he states that the Lord has separated himself who is faithful and will hear his cry.

outline.title: Holy response to the disturbance
outline.explanation: Instead of letting the wrath dominate, the righteous must reflect in silence, in the inside, and not sin. The right way is to offer sacrifices of righteousness and remain trusting in the Lord.

outline.title: The Search for the good and peace granted by God
outline.explanation: Many seek some visible prosperity, but David asks for the light of the Lord's face. This divine approval produces joy greater than the abundance of wheat and wine and leads to safe rest.

study.context: The text presents David speaking to the Lord and also addressing the men around him. The given notes indicate that the psalm may have been used in the cult, delivered to the regent, and Adam Clarke suggests that it was composed in the same period of the previous psalm, amid the rebellion of Absalom, understanding it as a night anthem. This last historical connection appears as an interpretation, not as an indisputable statement of the psalm itself. The musical title shows that the poem had a community and liturgical function, not just private.
study.theology: The psalm teaches that godly life involves tension between human opposition and divine trust. God is called the God of my righteousness, indicating that the righteousness and restoration of the psalmist depend on the Lord Himself. Also appears the idea that God separates the faithful to himself, that is, recognizes and guards those who belong to him. The text shows that holiness is not only religious emotion: it includes self-control, silent reflection and just practices. There is also a spiritual critique of false happiness based on prosperity or appearance of success; true joy comes from God's favor, described as the light of his face. The outcome of the psalm links inner peace, physical rest and spiritual security to the protection of the Lord.

scholarViews.insight: Angry passions should not rule the righteous; instead, he reflects in silence before acting, and this gathering opens up space to trust in the Lord.
The desire of "bem." is often poorly oriented: many seek only prosperity and sensitive satisfaction, rather than turning to God, who is the only one capable of granting the true good.
Rest in peace depends on the trust in the Lord, which gives the psalmist an inner and outer security to lie down and sleep without fear.

questions: What changes in the way of sleeping and resting when trust in God is stronger than the pressure of circumstances?
In what situations do I usually react in haste or irritation, rather than meditate in silence before the Lord?
What types of "bem" have I sought with more intensity: God's approval or passing advantages?
study.practice: Separate a moment at the end of the day to do what the psalm guides: to recognize the anguish before God, to silence the heart for a few minutes, to examine whether there was anger or anxiety that can turn sin, and then surrender the night to the Lord in simple prayer. Seek also to align your decisions with justice, not just the appearance of success. The practical application of the psalm is to learn to rest without depending on the total control of the circumstances.
study.uncertainty: The psalm does not explicitly inform the historical occasion of its composition. The connection with Absalom's rebellion, mentioned by a commentator, is an interpretative proposal and not a certain data of the text. Nor is it possible to affirm, only on the basis of the given notes, whether the expression on the "light of the face" should be understood exclusively as favor, blessing or both; the notes point to favor and peace, without exhausting the meaning.
